definition: Enclave means a distinct community or territory lying entirely inside a larger one.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word enclave. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know enclave should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Lesotho is that rarest of things, a national enclave — an entire country lying wholly inside a single neighbor.
A quarter — like a city's theater quarter — has a name and a flavor, but its edges stay open; it stops short of an enclave's real enclosure.
Citadel goes further than enclave — an enclave is distinct and enclosed; a citadel is fortified, holding the world outside at spearpoint.

A pocket is a small, isolated patch of something spread thin — a pocket of fog, of resistance, of poverty. It is loose and informal, and it has no fixed edge. An enclave is bounded and lasting: a real community or territory with a line around it that a map can draw.

Island, used figuratively, is anything wholly surrounded by what it is not — an island of calm in a loud house. It borrows the shape of an enclave but none of the substance: an enclave is an actual community or territory whose boundary and difference are really there.

Whatever surrounds it — another country, another language, another way of life — the enclave sits wholly inside it and stays distinct, a sealed pocket rather than a blurred edge.
Enclave is precise where neighborhood and district are loose: it says surrounded, bounded, and different from what surrounds it.
Maps use it for territory — one nation's land inside another — and reporters use it for communities that keep their own language or ways.
If nothing encloses it, it is just a district.

Ask a cab driver for 'the Basque block,' and you will be delivered to a three-street enclave that has sat inside the city's downtown since the 1910s.
It is not a theme or a marketing district: the boundary follows the original parish line, and inside it the bakery, the handball court, and the language school all run as they did a century ago.
City maps print the line; deeds and parish records defend it.
Developers have nibbled at every neighborhood around it, but each attempt to build across the line has died in a drawer at the historical commission.
Outside, the downtown churns and rebrands itself every decade; inside, the same three streets keep their own time.
